extracted.intended_audience: poets and writers interested in composing epistolary (letter) poetry; literate readers of The Spectator
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing verse-letters (epistles) in two classical modes (the Ovidian love/mournful manner and the Horatian familiar/critical/moral manner), including what qualities each mode requires and how to handle lofty subjects in the epistolary form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of epistolary poetry (Ovidian vs Horatian)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epistolary poetry is a species of poetry by itself and may be reduced into two classes: (1) the Ovidian way — love-letters, letters of friendship, and letters on mournful occasions; (2) the Horatian way — familiar, critical, and moral Epistles, with additions of letters of mirth and humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the class appropriate to subject and temperament: Ovidian for delicate, tender, passionate topics; Horatian for social critique, moral reflection, wit, and familiar satire. The author gives Ovid and Horace as the principal models for each class respectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for the Ovidian epistolary style
rubrics_metrics.description: Success in the Ovidian manner depends less on wit than on the delicacy and tenderness of sentiment; versification should be soft, with flowing, querulous numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before attempting this style, the writer should examine whether his own passions (especially gentler passions) are naturally easy and susceptible; cultivate delicate, tender feeling over cleverness. Avoid harsh or laboured verse; aim for smooth, plaintive cadences that evoke feeling rather than displaying ingenuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications for the Horatian epistolary style
rubrics_metrics.description: To excel after Horace one must possess a good fund of strong, masculine sense; thorough knowledge of mankind; insight into the business and prevailing humours of the age; a mind seasoned with moral precepts; refined reflections on life's bright and dark sides; mastery of refined raillery; and an understanding of the delicacies and absurdities of conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine lively wit with an easy, concise manner of expression and a free, disengaged tone that shows the writer as a man of the world rather than a recluse. Draw illustrations, comparisons, and images from common life. Judiciously insert strokes of satire, criticism, and panegyric 'by the by' to enliven the composition. The Horatian epistle should be instructive as well as entertaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone, diction, and versification — avoid prose and vulgar diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when writing familiar epistles, the poet must not fall into prose or vulgar diction merely because the style is informal; as verse, the epistle requires careful versification and elevated expression where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain poetic form and care for versification. Use plain or coarse diction only when the nature and humour of the subject necessarily require it. The author notes that some critics find Horace occasionally careless in versification; the modern epistolary poet should take more than ordinary care to keep poetic qualities intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling sublime or high subjects in the epistolary form
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects of the most sublime nature can be treated advantageously in the epistolary way (e.g., Horace's epistle to Augustus), producing a mix of familiarity and grandeur where the poet seems surprised by the subject and partly led into it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the dignity of the subject urges descriptions and sentiments that appear unpremeditated, allow the poetical voice to swell into grandeur and then gracefully recollect into the natural style of a letter. The effect can resemble an 'Incognito' visit of a king: lofty subject-matter benefits from a blend of intimacy and pomp; the poet should balance inspiration-driven passages with conversational ease.
